title: Multi-Asset Liquidation in Dark Pools with Adverse Selection

p.t: Every trading day, substantial volumes are excecuted in dark pools -alternative trading venues that match buyers and sellers without revealing order information until completion. While such venues mitigate price impact, they expose traders to adverse selection risk, as counterparties may possess superior information. In practice, portfolio liquidation and execution problems typically involve multiple correlated assets. However, despite the empirical relevance of both adverse selection and multi-asset trading, the existing stochastic control literature treats these features largely in isolation: models incorporating adverse selection are predominantly single-asset, whereas multi-asset models often abstract from adverse selection effects. For example, Kratz and Schöneborn [23] analyze discrete-time multi-asset liquidation without adverse selection; the single-asset case with absolute-value adverse selection costs is treated in [23,Section 5] and further extended in [25]. Continuous-time multi-asset models with dark pools were considered in [24] again without adverse selection. The single-asset version of [24] was extended by Kratz [22], incorporating absolute-value adverse selection costs, with motivation from [16]. In [16], Horst and Naujokat solve the single-asset liquidation problem in dark pools and in a two-sided limit order market with linear adverse selection and singular trading strategies, using the stochastic maximum principle. Cheridito and Sepin [8] study discrete-time liquidation with adverse selection, stochastic volatility and stochastic liquidity, however, in the single-asset setting. Klöck et al [21] investigate market impact in dark pools and derive conditions to exclude price manipulation, concluding that adverse-selection costs should be at least quadratic. Quadratic costs in dark pools were later exploited in, e.g., Graewe et al [12,13], Horst and Xia [18] and Kruse and Popier [27]. For multi-asset liquidation (execution) problems, see, e.g., [1,2,3,15,17,20,28,33].

To the best of our knowledge, multi-asset liquidation in dark pools with adverse selection costs remains an unsolved problem in literature, despite being highly relevant in stochastic control theory and mathematical finance. Motivated by this gap, in this paper we study a multidimensional stochastic control problem arising in liquidation in dark pools with adverse selection. In liquidation problems, the assumption of linear temporary price impact-leading to a quadratic cost functional-is well established in the literature; see, for example, [4]. To maintain mathematical tractability, we adopt several simplifying assumptions regarding dark-pool trading, which is considerably more complex in practice. First, since execution times in a dark pool are inherently uncertain, we follow the standard approach in the liquidation literature with dark pools (e.g., [16,24]) and model executions as the jump times of Poisson processes, with each jump corresponding to a single execution. Second, we allow for dynamic updating of dark-pool orders: the trader may adjust order sizes continuously over time without restrictions such as a minimum resting time. Third, we assume an all-or-nothing execution mechanism with no partial fills; whenever the Poisson process jumps, the outstanding dark-pool order is fully executed. Finally, we model dark-pool adverse selection costs in a reduced quadratic form. This specification is consistent with the single-asset framework in [13], but differs from alternative modeling choices in the literature. For instance, [22] adopts an absolute-value cost, which results in a non-linear-quadratic control problem that is currently tractable only in the single-asset case. Another approach is taken in [16], where adverse selection costs are linear; however, this formulation is meaningful only in a two-sided limit order book setting. Beyond mathematical tractability, the use of quadratic adverse selection costs enables our model to capture information spillover effects in dark-pool trading. By dark-pool information spillover, we mean that a dark-pool execution in one asset may transmit information to the price dynamics of another asset-for example, because the counterparty infers information about related fundamentals.

As a consequence of the above modeling choices, we formulate the liquidation problem as the following multidimensional linear-quadratic stochastic control problem: where the dynamics X, controlled by (ξ, β), satisfies Here, x 0 ∈ R n denotes the initial position across n assets. The process ξ represents the trading rate in the primary exchange, while β denotes the dynamically adjusted passive orders submitted to the dark pool. Moreover, N = (N 1 , ..., N n ) is an n-dimensional Poisson process; each jump of N i corresponds to the execution of the dark-pool order in asset i. The symbol ⊙ denotes the Hadamard product 1 . In the cost functional (1.1), the first two terms are standard in the liquidation literature and represent temporary price impact and inventory risk, respectively. The final term reflects the reduced-form quadratic specification of adverse selection costs discussed above. In particular, the diagonal elements of Γ capture own-asset adverse selection, whereas the off-diagonal elements Γ ij represents spillover effect from asset i to asset j, potentially arising from common toxic counterparties. We solve a general version of (1.1)-(1.2) with random coefficients by analyzing a matrix-valued backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE) with Poisson jumps and a singular terminal value induced by the liquidation constraint X T = 0. Our first contribution is to establish the welllposedness of this novel BSDE. It is well known that the main difficulty in multidimensional BSDEs lies in the failure of a general comparison principle. To overcome this issue, we are inspired by the linearization technique in [30,Section 5] and appropriately linearize the original BSDE. We show that the resulting linearized equation admits a unique positive semidefinite solution. Owing to the presence of Poisson jumps, our analysis is considerably more involved than that in [30]. We interpret this linearization result as a comparison principle and demonstrate that it is more powerful than existing ones for analyzing similar equations with singular terminal values; see the subsequent discussion for a detailed comparison. We emphasize that both the existence and the uniqueness results rely crucially on this comparison principle. To establish existence, we approximate the singular terminal condition by a sequence of finite truncations and derive sharp a-priori estimates for the corresponding truncated equations using the established comparison principle.

We then let the truncation level tend to infinity. The careful a-priori estimates ensure convergence of the sequence, and the limit is verified to be one solution of the original matrix-valued BSDE with singular terminal value. Compared with the existence result, the uniqueness result is even more significant. In the literature on BSDEs with singular terminal conditions-no matter in the one-dimensional or multidimensional setting-uniqueness typically remains unresolved. To the best of our knowledge, our result provides the first uniqueness theorem for matrix-valued BSDEs with singular terminal conditions, even in the absence of jumps, and the second uniqueness result for multidimensional BSDEs with singular terminal conditions; the first was obtained in our previous work [10], which establishes uniqueness for a system of BSDEs with singular terminal values arising from optimal liquidation under liquidity regime switching. To prove uniqueness, we follow the approach developed in [10], which in turn builds on ideas from [13]. We first show that the solution constructed as the limit of the truncated sequence is the minimal solution, in the sense that any other solution dominates it pointwise. Most existing works stop at this minimality property. In contrast, we proceed further. We solve the associated stochastic control problem and characterize the value function via the constructed solution. We then show that the quadratic form associated with any matrix-valued solution is bounded above by the value function, and hence by the quadratic form corresponding to the constructed solution. This yields the reverse inequality and establishes uniqueness. The comparison principle again plays a central role in deriving this key estimate. Moreover, a further key step in proving the reverse inequality is to show that any solution to the BSDE with singular terminal value admits a uniformly positive definite lower bound.

To the best of our knowledge, there is no existing study on multi-asset liquidation in dark pools with adverse selection. Consequently, the interaction between multiple assets and adverse selection has remained unexplored in the literature. As our second contribution, we investigate the interplay among asset correlation (stemming from the multi-asset structure), adverse selection, and spillover effects (arising jointly from adverse selection and cross-asset interactions) in a two-asset model with constant parameters. In particular, we analyze how well-and poorly diversified portfolios are affected by adverse selection and spillover effects. To isolate and highlight this interaction, we abstract from cross-impact effects by assuming that the cross-impact matrix is diagonal. Theoretically, we show that the behavior of a well-diversified portfolio (see Definition 5.2) is governed by the trade-off between the hedging effect induced by asset correlation and the spillover effect in dark-pool trading. Specifically, a well-diversified portfolio reduces costs and remains protected until liquidation if and only if the spillover effect is dominated by the hedging effect. Furthermore, we find adverse selection primarily affects whether an initially poorly diversified portfolio can be transformed into a well-diversified one through dark-pool trading. Our paper relates to several strands of the literature. First, a central feature of liquidation problems in stochastic control is the singular terminal value of the value function induced by the liquidation constraint. Depending on whether one adopts the dynamic programming principle or the stochastic maximum principle, this leads to a PDE, BSDE, or ODE with a singular terminal value; see the pioneering works [5,11,13,17,27,31,32]. All of these contributions focus on one-dimensional equations. Results for multidimensional BSDEs with singular terminal values remain scarce. Relevant works include Kratz and Schöneborn [24], Horst and Xia [17], and the recent paper by Ackermann et al. [1]. Among these, [17] studies multi-asset liquidation with transient price impact but without dark-pool trading, leading to a matrix-valued BSDE without jumps. The recent work [1] analyzes a broad class of multidimensional linear-quadratic stochastic control problems with random unbounded coefficients and general terminal state constraints, again without dark-pool trading, resulting in matrix-valued BSDEs without jumps.

Our techniques differ from each other; [1] uses the comparison principle in [17] that is not sufficient to our setting. Our model is closest to [24], which considers multi-asset liquidation with dark-pool trading but without adverse selection. In that setting, all coefficients are constant, and the problem reduces to an ODE with a singular terminal value. Beyond introducing and solving a new matrix-valued BSDE with jumps, our most significant theoretical contribution-relative to nearly all of the aforementioned worksis the establishment of a uniqueness result. Uniqueness for BSDEs with singular terminal conditions is rare in the literature, particularly in the multidimensional setting. To the best of our knowledge, the only exceptions are [13,14,18,10]: the first three treat one-dimensional equations, while the last addresses a system of BSDEs arising from regime switching. Accordingly, our result provides the first uniqueness theorem for matrix-valued BSDEs with singular terminal conditions. Importantly, this contribution remains new even in substantially simpler settings. In particular, uniqueness is not available in the literature even when jumps are removed, nor when all coefficients are constant so that the BSDE reduces to an ODE. The significance of this point is illustrated in [24,Remark 3.7], where the corresponding ODE, constituting a special case of our BSDE with constant coefficients and without adverse selection, is shown only to admit a principal solution. Our results confirm that this principal solution is in fact unique.

If the liquidation constraint is relaxed and instead the terminal open position is penalized, the problem leads to a matrix-valued BSDE with jumps and a finite terminal value. A second line of research closely related to our work concerns multidimensional BSDEs with jumps; see, for example, [6,7,19,26,29,35]. Our contribution differs from these works in that we establish a powerful comparison principle for multidimensional BSDEs, which plays a central role in both the existence and uniqueness analysis. In [6,7], the driver is required to be Lipschitz continuous in (y, z, ψ). Our BSDE does not satisfy this condition a-priori, since uniform boundedness of (Y, Ψ) is not immediate. Establishing such boundedness, however, itself relies on a comparison principle for multidimensional BSDEs. This tool is not available in [6,7]; in particular, [6] proves a comparison principle only in the one-dimensional setting. The work [26] studies multidimensional BSDEs under general filtrations with monotone drivers, a structure related to ours. However, the comparison principle established there is again restricted to the one-dimensional case. In [19], two comparison principles for multidimensional BSDEs are derived, but they rely on componentwise comparison and therefore cannot be applied to our matrix-valued setting. The paper [29] establishes well-posedness for a broad class of multidimensional BSDEs with jumps under general filtrations and random horizons. Although our driver may satisfy their structural assumptions, this holds only after boundedness of Y and Ψ has been established-an argument that again depends on our comparison principle. Moreover, the comparison result in [29] is also limited to the one-dimensional case. Finally, [35] analyzes general matrix-valued BSDEs with jumps using Doob-Meyer decomposition and inverse-flow techniques. Their approach does not rely on comparison principles and does not require apriori estimates as precise as those needed in our setting. By contrast, our analysis hinges on a comparison principle tailored to the matrix-valued structure of the equation. The strength of our comparison principle is further illustrated by comparison with the penalized problem in [24], which corresponds to a special case of our BSDE when the coefficients are constant and adverse selection is absent. In that setting, well-posedness is obtained only under the additional assumption that the penalization parameter is sufficiently large. Our comparison principle allows us to remove this restrictive condition. When this paper was near completion, we became aware of the very interesting work [9], in which Ding et al. study a matrix-valued BSDE arising from an indefinite linear-quadratic control problem with jumps. Our truncated BSDE is included there as a special case. They construct a strongly regular solution, which turns out to be maximal among all strongly regular solutions. Our approach is different and we focus on the search for nonnegative solutions. A priori, nonnegative solutions and strongly regular solutions do not imply each other. However, after proving in Lemma 3.4 that any nonnegative solution is in fact uniformly positive definite, we deduce that our nonnegative solution is strongly regular. This uniform positivity result is not an immediate consequence of the methods in [9]. Moreover, for the analysis of our subsequent BSDE with singular terminal values, we need precise upper and lower bounds for the solution of the truncated BSDE, which are not required in [9]. In addition, our uniqueness result (even for the truncated BSDE) relies crucially on Lemma 3.4 and partially confirms the uniqueness claim made in [9, Remark 5.10].

Finally, our work is closely related to the literature on optimal liquidation. Our primary benchmark is [24], which studies multi-asset liquidation with dark-pool trading but without adverse selection. In that setting, dark-pool trading is effectively costless, so asset correlation is the sole channel through which costs interact across assets. In particular, when the temporary impact matrix is diagonal, a well-diversified portfolio naturally reduces total costs and is therefore protected throughout liquidation. Likewise, a poorly diversified portfolio can be transformed into a well-diversified one through dark-pool trading so as to mitigate correlation-induced costs. Once adverse selection is introduced, however, dark-pool trading becomes costly and an additional interaction channel emerges through spillover effects. We rigorously show that the outcome is determined by the trade-off between the hedging effect arising from asset correlation and the spillover effect in dark-pool trading. In particular, diversification is no longer uniformly beneficial; its effectiveness depends on the relative strength of these two forces. These interactions cannot be captured in models with multiple assets but without adverse selection, such as [24], nor in single-asset models with adverse selection, such as [22]. Our results therefore complement and extend the existing literature, especially [24], by demonstrating how adverse selection fundamentally reshapes the role of diversification in multi-asset liquidation. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we introduce the notation used throughout the paper. In Section 3, we relax the liquidation constraint by penalizing the terminal open position and analyze the resulting unconstrained stochastic control problem. In particular, we establish the comparison principle that is crucial for the subsequent analysis. In Section 4, we prove the existence of a solution to the matrix-valued BSDE with jumps and a singular terminal condition. This result relies on the a-priori estimates developed in Section 3, especially the comparison principle. Building on this solution, Section 4 also solves the stochastic control problem (1.1)-(1.2). More importantly, we establish the uniqueness of the solution to the matrix-valued BSDE with singular terminal condition. Finally, in Section 5, we consider a two-asset specification to highlight the interaction between multiple assets and adverse selection.

In the subsequent subsections, we examine the trade-off between the hedging effect and the spillover effect from several perspectives. First, we show that a well-diversified portfolio reduces costs only when the hedging effect dominates the spillover effect. Second, we demonstrate that such a portfolio remains protected throughout the liquidation process only if the hedging effect outweighs the spillover effect. These results contrast sharply with [24], where, in the absence of adverse selection-and hence without spillover effects-a well-diversified portfolio always reduces costs and remains protected during liquidation.

p.t: Proposition 4.5 in [24] shows that, in the absence of adverse selection, a portfolio has lower costs if and only if it is well diversified. A well-diversified portfolio reduces costs when the hedging and spillover effects reinforce each other, that is, when ργ 12 ≥ 0. p.s: Is a poorly diversified portfolio rescued by optimal dark pool trading?
p.t: If γ i ̸ = 0, the sign of a poorly diversified portfolio is not always flipped by (5.13). Thus, γ i contributes to rescuing poorly diversifiled portfolio. The presence of adverse selection makes the trader less aggressive in using dark-pool orders to convert a poorly diversified portfolio into a well-diversified one. Without adverse selection, every poorly diversified portfolio would be rescued through dark-pool executions. However, according to condition (5.13), when adverse selection is present, only a severely poorly diversified portfolio can be turned into a well-diversified one via dark-pool trading. The intuition is straightforward. When γ i ̸ = 0, dark-pool executions entail adverse-selection costs. A trader will choose to overturn the sign of her position through dark-pool orders only if the reduction in portfolio risk achieved by restoring diversification outweighs the expected adverse-selection losses, that is, only when the portfolio is sufficiently poorly diversified. With moderate mis-diversification, it is cheaper to remain partially hedged than to incur large adverse-selection costs.
